sections.sectionText: How to Read and Write like Cleopatra. his class introduces the technology of reading and writing available in the lifetime of Cleopatra, and also the most common educational practices of that time. Students will learn to make and use several of the writing media that were dominant before the printing press (wax tablets, clay tablets, papyrus paper, ink), and they will see how people approached learning to read and write when skills like memory and improvisation were integral to the process. The main focus will be Egypt in the 1st century BCE, but related places and times will be discussed.

Wonders of the World In this class you will study the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World: the Great Pyramid of Giza, Hanging Gardens of Babylon, Temple of Artemis at Ephesus, Statue of Zeus at Olympia, Mausoleum at Halicarnassus, Colossus of Rhodes, and the Lighthouse of Alexandria. You will learn how they were made, what they meant to the people who built them, and the ways they have influenced modern art and architecture. Field trips to architectural wonders on the UIUC campus will enrich our understanding of the past.

Wonders of the Ancient World. In this class you will study the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World: the Great Pyramid of Giza, Hanging Gardens of Babylon, Temple of Artemis at Ephesus, Statue of Zeus at Olympia, Mausoleum at Halicarnassus, Colossus of Rhodes, and the Lighthouse of Alexandria. You will learn how they were made, what they meant to the people who built them, and the ways they have influenced modern art and architecture. Field trips to architectural wonders on the UIUC campus will enrich our understanding of the past.

Nightmares of Nero. Few Roman emperors have been so constantly reviled in history and popular culture as Nero. Ancient sources depict him as a deviant, a larger-than-life monster, a tyrant, a megalomaniac, an arsonist, a murderer. Early Christians demonized him as their greatest persecutor, and apocalyptic prophecies identified him with the Antichrist. Setting its sights on the various myths and exaggerations that have come down to us about Nero, this course explores the question of what we can know of the infamous emperor and the age that bears his name. Particular emphasis will be placed on the nightmarish refractions of Neronian Rome found in the works of Seneca, Lucan, and Petronius.

Pompeii: Life in a Roman City. Pompeii, a city in the Bay of Naples famously destroyed but uniquely preserved by the eruption of Mt. Vesuvius in 79 CE, has traditionally been viewed as the quintessential example of the ancient Roman urban experience. But just how ‘Roman’ was Pompeii? This class examines how evidence from Pompeii contributes to our knowledge of Roman material culture and the everyday use of urban space; and questions whether our broader conception of Roman life is limited by our reliance on evidence from this one city. In answering such questions, we will deepen our understanding of what it meant to be Roman in the ancient Mediterranean world.

Thinking about Trauma through Athenian Drama: Ancient theater offered the space for reflecting upon the violence and trauma for its original audiences and for contemporary societies. This course focuses on the experiences of the ancients with war, trauma, and the plight of veterans, prisoners of war, and refugees. It also looks beyond Athenian theater to modern adaptations by theater companies, playwrights, directors and speaks to modern issues, making the plays respond to the ravages of contemporary wars, the experience of refugees, and gender violence: allowing them to speak directly to communities of color and issues of social justice. Readings include both ancient Greek plays and modern adaptations of select plays.

subject: CWL
title: Modern Masterpieces of Western Culture
degreeAttributes: Advanced Composition, Humanities - Lit & Arts, and Cultural Studies - Western course.

sections.sectionText: Through a comparative study of some of the “top hits” of modern literature from the 17th century until today, we will get at some of the most vexing questions facing us as humans. This course asks you to think about how culture develops “horizontally” (i.e., chronologically) through time, building on and responding to what has come before it. Yet, culture also develops “vertically” (i.e., attending to hierarchies), with relation to class, gender, race, and other structures of power that influence whose words reach large audiences and whose don’t. In this course, we will think about both of these dynamics at play as we encounter works of literature across a variety of genres and literary movements contained under the charged term of “Modern Masterpieces of Western Culture.” Some authors covered include Jonathan Swift, Mary Shelly, Fyodor Dostoevsky, Joseph Conrad, Franz Kafka, and China Miéville.

sections.sectionText: SP27 ENGL 202 / CWL 253 / MDVL 201 - Medieval Literature and Culture - Carson Koepke - In this course, we will explore the literary and cultural diversity of the Middle Ages by reading and analyzing narratives from Africa, Asia, Europe, and Mesoamerica around the turn of the first millennium. We will experience how medieval peoples thought about physical and metaphysical travel, how they retold epic myths and origin stories, and how the genre of the medieval romance laid the foundations for the modern novel. Readings (in Modern English translation) will be sourced from a wide variety of religious and linguistic traditions, including Old English, Arabic, Coptic, Chinese, Persian, Japanese, Old Norse, and K'iche' Mayan. As we read, we will work to place narratives like "Beowulf" and "The Tale of Genji" within their wider cultural contexts while also thinking critically about what features and practices unite literature across cultures.

subject: CWL
title: Grimm's Fairy Tales in Context
degreeAttributes: Humanities - Lit & Arts, and Cultural Studies - Western course.
info: Same as ENGL 266 and GER 251. See GER 251.

sections.sectionText: GER 251 / ENGL 266 / CWL 254 The Grimms’ Fairy Tales in Context Students read classical and little-known tales from the Grimms' 19th-century collections, as well as earlier tales and other texts, focusing on how power, gender, race, class, and ecological issues play out in these surprisingly dense, meaningful, and very old stories. Why do we continue to tell these tales? Why do certain stories recur again and again, in Western and other cultures? The power of narrative is at the center of our lives, and of these tales, and by the end of the semester we will understand this power much better. This course fulfills General Education requirements in Literature and the Arts, and in Western and Comparative Culture.

sections.sectionText: SP27 ENGL 206 / CWL 257 - Enlightenment Literature and Culture - Hina Nazar - Have you ever wondered what people mean when they say that the United States is a child of the Enlightenment, or that the Enlightenment is under attack by nativist forces, or that we need to return to Enlightenment values? This course enables you to engage such statements knowledgeably by providing a broad-based introduction to the Enlightenment, a multifaceted cultural and intellectual development of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries (roughly the period 1650-1800). While many of you are probably familiar with key texts and figures of the American Enlightenment, this course focuses on the European—and, more particularly, the British—Enlightenment, which preceded the founding of the United States. In the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, Europe witnessed unprecedented social, economic, political, and cultural changes that collectively produced a giant leap toward the world we inhabit today. It was an Age of Revolution and of newfound faith in the rights of the individual though these rights were by no means extended to all. It was an Age of Reason, of tremendous advances in science and technology, though reason was by no means the only altar at which so-called enlightened individuals worshipped: God and sentiment remained powerful forces throughout the long eighteenth century. We will consider how the modern mindset that is associated with the Enlightenment was developed by some of the most significant texts of the period, and how it challenged traditional understandings of duty and humanity’s place in the world. Our readings are divided into four modules. After an overview of the Enlightenment spirit in Module 1, we will dig deeper into such crucial concerns of the period as property, race, and empire (Module 2); morality or virtue (Module 3); and education (Module 4). Gender figures prominently in all four modules since women were finding a public voice and entering the literary marketplace in unprecedented numbers at this time. As the moment in history that is credited with creating the modern world, the Enlightenment continues to speak to us today—as is evidenced by its continued currency in public discourse—and our aim this semester is not only to understand its core values but also to link them with our own.

subject: CWL
title: Lit Genres and Forms
info: 3 undergraduate hours. 3 or 4 graduate hours. May be repeated to a maximum of 9 undergraduate hours or 12 graduate hours. Prerequisite: One year of college literature or consent of instructor.

sections.sectionText: We live in stories. These stories come to us most often in mediated collections: a treasury of bedtime stories; a famous writer's selected works; a list of texts on a syllabus; a queue of new episodes to stream. We might consider all of these as modes of the anthology, a term that comes from the Greek anthos (flower) and legein (to gather): a bouquet of flowers, gathered up together for our enjoyment. Despite its ubiquity, the anthology remains surprisingly under-theorized. This course explores the anthology form and what the collection, organization, and dissemination of texts does for literature itself. Is the anthology a graveyard where literary works, severed from their living contexts, are buried? What is the relationship between the anthology and other forms, including the novel, short story, poem, and excerpt? What is the relationship between the anthology and the reader? Together, we will interrogate this form, its affordances, and its limitations. Some of our theoretical readings will approach the anthology with attention to: New Formalism (Caroline Levine) Rhizomatic interconnectivity (Deleuze and Guattari) Collecting (Walter Benjamin) Reader-response theory (Wolfgang Iser) Print capitalism (Benedict Anderson) Cultural capital and canon-making (John Guillory) Course assignments will focus on developing practical scholarly skills, including how to write a book review, respond to a Call for Papers (CFP), present at an academic conference, and give an effective peer review.

title: Historiography of Cinema
info: Same as ENGL 503 and MACS 503. See MACS 503.

sections.sectionText: While the title of this course is "Historiography of Cinema," it is designed to incorporate issues of moving image culture more broadly. Cinema studies provides the longest and most thorough discourse on moving image culture, and therefore this course introduces methodology and theory beneficial to students working on topics in television, video art, advertising, and digital media-making, and more. The aim of this class is to introduce and train students in research methods and approaches in moving image studies, and discuss how the long tradition of cinematic scholarly discourse can impact research in other areas of media and various periods of technological emergence. Each class session includes a screening (usually about 90 min) of a film appropriate to the following week's reading.

sections.sectionText: Located at the intersection of Africa, Europe, and the Middle East, North Africa has long been a site of contact and exchange between diverse peoples and cultures. This course will offer students a wide-ranging introduction to North African cultures and to the academic field of North African studies. Particular emphasis will be placed on reading recent scholarship in order to introduce students to major debates in the field. Some of the topics will include: European colonialism and its legacies in North Africa; ethnic and racial categories; religious communities and identities; gender and sexuality; language use and linguistic identities; popular culture; and historical and cultural connections between North Africa and other regions throughout the world. To address these topics, the course syllabus will feature a diverse array of cultural texts as well as scholarship on North Africa from many disciplinary perspectives (including literary and cultural studies, history, anthropology, and area studies).
